To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) stand age can be estimated from Landsat TM imagery; (2) aboveground biomass can be estimated from lidar; (3) stand age and biomass can be used to calculate NPPAw; (4) NPPAw can be used to estimate NPP; (5) NPP estimates made using this technique compare well to estimates made from a process model; and (6) NPP estimates from this technique are significantly different than estimates made from the process model.

(1) lidar-based estimates of stand age and aboveground biomass are highly correlated with field inventory estimates and (2) NPPAw estimates derived from lidar estimates of stand age, aboveground biomass and stand age change are significantly different from estimates derived from a spatially extensive process model.

1) NPPAw can be estimated from lidar-based biomass and Landsat-based stand age; 2) NPPAw estimates from this method are comparable to inventory-based estimates and are different from estimates from a spatial biogeochemistry NPP model; 3) this method can be used for validation of spatial NPP estimates from biogeochemistry and process models; and 4) this method is applicable to regions with stand replacing disturbance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the validation of remote sensing estimates of forest NPP.
the development of a new, independent method for estimating NPPAw that can be used for validation of spatially extensive models of NPP and NEP.
the development of new approaches to estimating NPP and NEP at the landscape scale, and with their application to the validation of spatially extensive estimates of forest productivity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study presents a novel approach to estimating forest productivity that is based on stand age as a proxy for disturbance history and lidar estimates of canopy structure.
the method presented here can be used as a tool for validating NPP estimates from remote sensing and/or biogeochemistry modeling.
the study provides a novel approach for the estimation of NPPAW, which is based on stand age, biomass and lidar remote sensing data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed an independent approach to estimate aboveground net primary productivity (NPPAW) that could be implemented at a regional scale.
this method is a promising approach for estimating NPPAw and for validating spatially extensive estimates from process based models.
this approach could provide an independent, spatially extensive estimate of NPPAw that could be used in model validation and in studies that require estimates of NPP over a large area.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the approach we describe is a potentially useful tool for validating estimates of NPP and NEP over large areas.

lidar estimates of biomass and stand age can be used to estimate forest productivity over large areas, and can be used for independent validation of spatially extensive estimates of forest productivity.
lidar and passive optical sensors can be combined to estimate NPPAw over large areas and that this approach can be used to validate spatially extensive flux estimates.
